Approximate Bellman Equations

The previous chapter replaced the value function by a parametric function v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\theta)v(⋅;θ) and asked which finite set of conditions should determine θ\thetaθ. This chapter asks how to compute θ\thetaθ, and when the result can be trusted. The answer that scales is also the simplest. Run value iteration, but after each application of the Bellman operator, fit the parametric function to the result. Each iteration is then an ordinary regression problem whose targets are Bellman backups, and any regressor can do the fitting: a grid interpolant, a tree ensemble, a neural network. This is fitted value iteration, and fitted Q-iteration, NFQ, DQN and NFQCA in the chapters ahead are elaborations of it.

The fit is not free. Value iteration converges because L\BellmanL is a contraction in the sup norm (Proposition 2), and the fit can undo that. The chapter therefore follows the algorithm with three results. If every fit is accurate to ε\varepsilonε, the errors do not accumulate beyond ε/(1−γ)\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)ε/(1−γ), which is what licenses an arbitrary regressor. Least squares can nonetheless make the errors grow without bound, on a two-state problem whose value function it represents exactly. And two kinds of fit are provably safe: averagers, which include grid interpolation and the tree ensembles of the first fitted Q-iteration algorithm, and least squares weighted by the state distribution of the policy being evaluated. Neural networks belong to neither kind. What keeps neural fitted Q-iteration stable in practice is a set of design choices that the fitted Q-iteration chapter examines. We then turn to the other solver of the previous chapter, Newton’s method, which becomes approximate policy iteration and, for linear features, the LSTD and LSPI algorithms. The chapter closes with the steps that separate fitted value iteration from NFQCA, and the chapter in which each is taken.

Learning Goals

After completing this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Write fitted value iteration for an arbitrary regressor, and recognize collocation and Galerkin projection as two choices of the fitting rule

  • Bound the error of fitted value iteration, and of its greedy policy, by the error of each fit

  • Construct a fitted value iteration that diverges, and state two conditions that prevent divergence: averagers in the sup norm, and on-policy weighting for policy evaluation

  • Explain approximate policy iteration as Newton’s method on the approximate Bellman equation, and LSTD and LSPI as its linear case

  • Name the steps from fitted value iteration to FQI, NFQ and NFQCA, and the chapter in which each is taken

Prerequisites: the weighted-residual template (previous chapter), the contraction and Newton-Kantorovich material of infinite-horizon MDPs, interpolation with cardinal functions in finite-horizon DP.

Fitted Value Iteration¶

What does value iteration become when the value function is stored as a parametric function rather than as a table?

Value iteration computes Lvk\Bellman v_kLvk​ at every state and stores the result. With a parametric function we can do neither, but we can do two things that together play the same role. We can evaluate the Bellman operator at finitely many states s1,…,sms_1, \ldots, s_ms1​,…,sm​,

yi=(Lvk)(si)=max⁡a∈Asi{r(si,a)+γ∑s′∈Sp(s′∣si,a) v(s′;θk)},y_i = (\Bellman v_k)(s_i) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_{s_i}} \Big\{ r(s_i,a) + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} p(s'|s_i,a)\, v(s';\theta_k) \Big\},yi​=(Lvk​)(si​)=a∈Asi​​max​{r(si​,a)+γs′∈S∑​p(s′∣si​,a)v(s′;θk​)},
(1)

and we can choose θk+1\theta_{k+1}θk+1​ so that v(⋅;θk+1)v(\cdot;\theta_{k+1})v(⋅;θk+1​) fits the pairs (si,yi)(s_i, y_i)(si​,yi​). The first step needs the model and the current function. The second is a supervised learning problem that knows nothing about Bellman equations.

Algorithm 1 (Fitted Value Iteration)

Inputs: States {si}i=1m\{s_i\}_{i=1}^m{si​}i=1m​ at which to compute targets, discount factor γ\gammaγ, function class {v(⋅;θ)}\{v(\cdot;\theta)\}{v(⋅;θ)}, fitting procedure fit\mathtt{fit}fit, tolerance ϵ\epsilonϵ

Output: Approximate value function v(⋅;θ)≈v∗v(\cdot;\theta) \approx v^*v(⋅;θ)≈v∗

  2. Set k←0k \leftarrow 0k←0

  3. repeat

  4. \quad for each state sis_isi​ do

  5. \quad\quad Compute target: yi←max⁡a∈Asi{r(si,a)+γ∑s′p(s′∣si,a) v(s′;θk)}y_i \leftarrow \displaystyle\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_{s_i}} \Big\{ r(s_i, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s_i, a)\, v(s';\theta_k) \Big\}yi​←a∈Asi​​max​{r(si​,a)+γs′∑​p(s′∣si​,a)v(s′;θk​)}

  6. \quad end for

  7. \quad Fit: θk+1←fit({(si,yi)}i=1m)\theta_{k+1} \leftarrow \mathtt{fit}\big(\{(s_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^m\big)θk+1​←fit({(si​,yi​)}i=1m​)

  8. \quad k←k+1k \leftarrow k+1k←k+1

  9. until ∥v(⋅;θk)−v(⋅;θk−1)∥<ϵ\|v(\cdot;\theta_k) - v(\cdot;\theta_{k-1})\| < \epsilon∥v(⋅;θk​)−v(⋅;θk−1​)∥<ϵ (or maximum iterations reached)

Write P\ProjP for the map that takes a function, through its values at s1,…,sms_1, \ldots, s_ms1​,…,sm​, to the fitted function. Then fitted value iteration is

vk+1=PLvk,v_{k+1} = \Proj \Bellman v_k,vk+1​=PLvk​,
(2)

value iteration with a fit after each sweep. Two choices define the algorithm: where the targets are computed, and how the function is fitted to them. Nothing depends on the max. Replacing L\BellmanL by the policy evaluation operator Lπ\BellmanPiLπ​ gives fitted policy evaluation, and replacing it by the smooth operator Lβ\mathrm{L}_\betaLβ​ of Regularized Bellman Operators gives fitted smooth value iteration. The weighted-residual methods of the previous chapter are two particular fitting rules.

Collocation and Galerkin as Fitting Rules¶

Collocation computes targets at exactly nnn states, as many as there are basis functions, and interpolates them: with Φ\boldsymbol{\Phi}Φ the n×nn \times nn×n matrix with entries Φij=φj(si)\Phi_{ij} = \varphi_j(s_i)Φij​=φj​(si​), the fit solves Φθk+1=y\boldsymbol{\Phi}\theta_{k+1} = yΦθk+1​=y. Here P\ProjP is the interpolation operator. With piecewise-linear cardinal functions on a grid, this is the stationary version of the interpolated backward recursion (16) of the finite-horizon chapter.

Algorithm 2 (Collocation with Function Iteration)

Input Collocation points {s1,…,sn}\{s_1, \ldots, s_n\}{s1​,…,sn​}, basis functions {φ1,…,φn}\{\varphi_1, \ldots, \varphi_n\}{φ1​,…,φn​}, initial θ(0)\theta^{(0)}θ(0), tolerance ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0

Output Converged coefficients θ∗\theta^*θ∗

  1. Form collocation matrix Φ\boldsymbol{\Phi}Φ with Φij=φj(si)\Phi_{ij} = \varphi_j(s_i)Φij​=φj​(si​)

  2. k←0k \leftarrow 0k←0

  3. repeat

    1. For each i=1,…,ni = 1, \ldots, ni=1,…,n:

      1. ti(k)←max⁡a∈Asi{r(si,a)+γ∑s′∈Sp(s′∣si,a)∑ℓ=1nθℓ(k)φℓ(s′)}t_i^{(k)} \leftarrow \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_{s_i}} \left\{ r(s_i, a) + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} p(s'|s_i, a) \sum_{\ell=1}^n \theta_\ell^{(k)} \varphi_\ell(s') \right\}ti(k)​←maxa∈Asi​​​{r(si​,a)+γ∑s′∈S​p(s′∣si​,a)∑ℓ=1n​θℓ(k)​φℓ​(s′)}

    2. Solve Φθ(k+1)=t(k)\boldsymbol{\Phi} \theta^{(k+1)} = t^{(k)}Φθ(k+1)=t(k)

    3. k←k+1k \leftarrow k + 1k←k+1

  4. until ∥θ(k)−θ(k−1)∥<ε\|\theta^{(k)} - \theta^{(k-1)}\| < \varepsilon∥θ(k)−θ(k−1)∥<ε

  5. return θ(k)\theta^{(k)}θ(k)

On the optimal stopping problem of the previous chapter, with n=4n = 4n=4 polynomial basis functions at Chebyshev nodes:

Source
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad

gamma = 0.9
n = 4

# Chebyshev nodes on [0, 1]
k = np.arange(1, n + 1)
nodes = 0.5 + 0.5 * np.cos((2*k - 1) * np.pi / (2*n))
nodes = np.sort(nodes)

# Vandermonde matrix
Phi = np.vander(nodes, n, increasing=True)

# Exact solution
v_bar_exact = (1 - np.sqrt(1 - gamma**2)) / gamma**2
s_star_exact = gamma * v_bar_exact
def v_exact(s):
    return np.where(s >= s_star_exact, s, gamma * v_bar_exact)

# Collocation iteration
theta = np.zeros(n)
print("Collocation iteration trace:")
print(f"{'Iter':<6} {'||theta||':<12} {'Max error':<12}")
print("-" * 30)

for iteration in range(60):
    def v_approx(s, th=theta):
        return sum(th[j] * s**j for j in range(n))
    v_bar, _ = quad(v_approx, 0, 1)
    test_points = np.linspace(0, 1, 100)
    max_error = max(abs(v_approx(s) - v_exact(s)) for s in test_points)
    if iteration % 5 == 0:
        print(f"{iteration:<6} {np.linalg.norm(theta):<12.6f} {max_error:<12.6f}")
    
    targets = np.maximum(nodes, gamma * v_bar)
    theta_new = np.linalg.solve(Phi, targets)
    if np.linalg.norm(theta_new - theta) < 1e-10:
        print(f"\nConverged in {iteration + 1} iterations; max error {max_error:.6f}")
        break
    theta = theta_new

The iteration converges linearly at the rate γ\gammaγ, as value iteration does, and the remaining error is the interpolation error of a cubic through four nodes on a function with a kink.

Galerkin projection fits by weighted least squares. Given a weight w(s)w(s)w(s) over states, θk+1\theta_{k+1}θk+1​ minimizes ∫(v(s;θ)−(Lvk)(s))2w(s) ds\int (v(s;\theta) - (\Bellman v_k)(s))^2 w(s)\,ds∫(v(s;θ)−(Lvk​)(s))2w(s)ds, whose first-order conditions are the Galerkin conditions ⟨v(⋅;θk+1)−Lvk,φi⟩w=0\langle v(\cdot;\theta_{k+1}) - \Bellman v_k, \varphi_i \rangle_w = 0⟨v(⋅;θk+1​)−Lvk​,φi​⟩w​=0, a linear system Mθk+1=b(k)M\theta_{k+1} = b^{(k)}Mθk+1​=b(k) with mass matrix Mij=⟨φi,φj⟩wM_{ij} = \langle \varphi_i, \varphi_j \rangle_wMij​=⟨φi​,φj​⟩w​ and bi(k)=⟨Lvk,φi⟩wb_i^{(k)} = \langle \Bellman v_k, \varphi_i \rangle_wbi(k)​=⟨Lvk​,φi​⟩w​. The integrals need quadrature. If the states sis_isi​ are drawn from www, the sample average replaces the integral and the fit becomes an ordinary least-squares regression on the pairs (si,yi)(s_i, y_i)(si​,yi​). Here P\ProjP is the www-orthogonal projection onto the span of the basis.

The two rules mark the ends of a range. Collocation computes few targets and matches them exactly; regression computes many and matches them on average. Regression is what scales, because it decouples the number of targets from the number of parameters and it applies unchanged to any model that can be fitted to data.

Fitting a Neural Network: Fixed Targets and the Semi-Gradient¶

For a model v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta)v(⋅;θ) that is nonlinear in its parameters, such as a neural network, the fit is

θk+1∈arg⁡min⁡θ∑i=1m(v(si;θ)−yi)2,yi=(Lvk)(si),\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k+1} \in \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \sum_{i=1}^m \big(v(s_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}) - y_i\big)^2, \qquad y_i = (\Bellman v_k)(s_i),θk+1​∈argθmin​i=1∑m​(v(si​;θ)−yi​)2,yi​=(Lvk​)(si​),
(3)

solved by gradient descent. Its first-order condition is again an orthogonality condition, with test functions that move with the parameters:

∑i=1m(v(si;θ)−yi)∂v(si;θ)∂θj=0for all j.\sum_{i=1}^m \big(v(s_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}) - y_i\big) \frac{\partial v(s_i;\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta_j} = 0 \quad \text{for all } j.i=1∑m​(v(si​;θ)−yi​)∂θj​∂v(si​;θ)​=0for all j.
(4)

The derivatives ∂v/∂θj\partial v/\partial\theta_j∂v/∂θj​ span the tangent space of the model at the current parameters. For a linear model they are the basis functions, and the condition is the sampled Galerkin condition. The targets yiy_iyi​ are held fixed during the fit, so the gradient differentiates only v(si;θ)v(s_i;\boldsymbol\theta)v(si​;θ) and never the operator. This is the semi-gradient of temporal difference learning. The least-squares criterion of Step 3: Impose Conditions on the Residual, Bellman residual minimization, would instead minimize ∑i(v(si;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(si))2\sum_i \big(v(s_i;\boldsymbol\theta) - (\Bellman v(\cdot;\boldsymbol\theta))(s_i)\big)^2∑i​(v(si​;θ)−(Lv(⋅;θ))(si​))2 with the same parameters on both sides. Its test functions, ∂v/∂θj−∂(Lv)/∂θj\partial v/\partial\theta_j - \partial(\Bellman v)/\partial\theta_j∂v/∂θj​−∂(Lv)/∂θj​, form the full gradient, and computing them requires differentiating through the max, by the envelope theorem, or through the log-sum-exp of the smooth Bellman operator. The two criteria have different solutions. Every algorithm in the chapters ahead, from NFQ to NFQCA, fits to fixed targets, and the fitted Q-iteration chapter studies what happens when the fit is warm-started and stopped after a few gradient steps instead of run to convergence.

Example: A Stopping Problem in Eight Dimensions¶

The stopping problem of the previous chapter has one state variable, and a grid of a dozen nodes solves it. To see why the fit matters, give the state DDD coordinates. An agent watches an index s∈[0,1]Ds \in [0,1]^Ds∈[0,1]D, for instance the prices of DDD assets. Stopping pays the average of the coordinates, sˉ=1D∑ℓsℓ\bar{s} = \frac{1}{D}\sum_\ell s_\ellsˉ=D1​∑ℓ​sℓ​, and ends the problem. Continuing pays nothing, and each coordinate then moves toward a fresh uniform draw, sℓ′=ρsℓ+(1−ρ)ξℓs'_\ell = \rho s_\ell + (1-\rho)\xi_\ellsℓ′​=ρsℓ​+(1−ρ)ξℓ​ with ξℓ∼U[0,1]\xi_\ell \sim U[0,1]ξℓ​∼U[0,1] independent and ρ=0.7\rho = 0.7ρ=0.7. The Bellman equation is

v∗(s)=max⁡{sˉ,  γ E[v∗(ρs+(1−ρ)ξ)]},γ=0.9.v^*(s) = \max\Big\{ \bar{s},\; \gamma\, \mathbb{E}\big[v^*(\rho s + (1-\rho)\xi)\big] \Big\}, \qquad \gamma = 0.9.v∗(s)=max{sˉ,γE[v∗(ρs+(1−ρ)ξ)]},γ=0.9.
(5)

The average sˉ\bar ssˉ is itself a Markov chain, sˉ′=ρsˉ+(1−ρ)ξˉ\bar{s}' = \rho\bar{s} + (1-\rho)\bar{\xi}sˉ′=ρsˉ+(1−ρ)ξˉ​, so v∗v^*v∗ depends on sss only through sˉ\bar ssˉ and can be computed exactly by one-dimensional value iteration. The algorithm does not know this. A grid with 11 nodes per axis has 11D11^D11D nodes: 121 for D=2D = 2D=2, 14,641 for D=4D = 4D=4, and 2.1×1082.1 \times 10^82.1×108 for D=8D = 8D=8, each needing an expectation over a DDD-dimensional successor at every iteration. Fitted value iteration instead computes targets at 2,000 states drawn uniformly from the cube, whatever DDD is, and fits them with an ensemble of extremely randomized trees Ernst et al. (2005) or with a neural network of two hidden layers. All three methods approximate the expectation by the average over the same 32 draws of ξ\xiξ, so they solve the same sample-average problem; the next chapter studies this approximation. The errors are measured against the exact v∗v^*v∗ at 5,000 fresh states.

The grid is the most accurate method while it fits in memory, and it is out of reach at D=8D = 8D=8. The trees and the network use the same 2,000 states in every dimension. The average error of the trees roughly doubles each time DDD doubles, while that of the network stays near 0.01; the figure shows that the network has found the one direction along which the value changes. Both have maximum errors several times their average, at the corners of the cube, where few of the sampled states lie. That gap is a first glimpse of the issue that dominates the analysis below and the batch methods of the fitted Q-iteration chapter: a fit is controlled where there are data, and only there.

How Fitting Errors Propagate¶

If every fit is only approximately right, how far from v∗v^*v∗ does fitted value iteration end, and how good is the policy it returns?

The finite-horizon chapter answered this for backward recursion with interpolation: with nonnegative weights, the error of the stored values is at most the sum of the interpolation errors of the later stages (Proposition 1). Over an infinite horizon the sum becomes a geometric series.

Theorem 1 (Error of approximate value iteration)

Let v0v_0v0​ be bounded and let the sequence vkv_kvk​ satisfy ∥vk+1−Lvk∥∞≤ε\|v_{k+1} - \Bellman v_k\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon∥vk+1​−Lvk​∥∞​≤ε for every kkk. Then

∥vk−v∗∥∞≤γk∥v0−v∗∥∞+ε1−γ.\|v_k - v^*\|_\infty \leq \gamma^k \|v_0 - v^*\|_\infty + \frac{\varepsilon}{1-\gamma}.∥vk​−v∗∥∞​≤γk∥v0​−v∗∥∞​+1−γε​.
(6)
Proof 1

Since v∗=Lv∗v^* = \Bellman v^*v∗=Lv∗ and L\BellmanL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction,

∥vk+1−v∗∥∞≤∥vk+1−Lvk∥∞+∥Lvk−Lv∗∥∞≤ε+γ∥vk−v∗∥∞.\|v_{k+1} - v^*\|_\infty \leq \|v_{k+1} - \Bellman v_k\|_\infty + \|\Bellman v_k - \Bellman v^*\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon + \gamma \|v_k - v^*\|_\infty.∥vk+1​−v∗∥∞​≤∥vk+1​−Lvk​∥∞​+∥Lvk​−Lv∗∥∞​≤ε+γ∥vk​−v∗∥∞​.
(7)

Unrolling the recursion gives ∥vk−v∗∥∞≤γk∥v0−v∗∥∞+ε(1+γ+⋯+γk−1)\|v_k - v^*\|_\infty \leq \gamma^k\|v_0 - v^*\|_\infty + \varepsilon(1 + \gamma + \cdots + \gamma^{k-1})∥vk​−v∗∥∞​≤γk∥v0​−v∗∥∞​+ε(1+γ+⋯+γk−1).

The value function is an instrument. What we use is the greedy policy, and its loss is bounded by the error of the value function it is greedy for Singh & Yee (1994).

Proposition 1 (Loss of a greedy policy)

If π\piπ is greedy with respect to vvv, that is Lπv=Lv\BellmanPi v = \Bellman vLπ​v=Lv, then

∥v∗−vπ∥∞≤2γ1−γ∥v−v∗∥∞.\|v^* - v_\pi\|_\infty \leq \frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\|v - v^*\|_\infty.∥v∗−vπ​∥∞​≤1−γ2γ​∥v−v∗∥∞​.
(8)
Proof 2

Let π∗\pi^*π∗ be an optimal policy. Then v∗−vπ=Lπ∗v∗−Lπvπv^* - v_\pi = \mathrm{L}_{\pi^*} v^* - \BellmanPi v_\piv∗−vπ​=Lπ∗​v∗−Lπ​vπ​, which we split as

v∗−vπ=(Lπ∗v∗−Lπ∗v)+(Lπ∗v−Lπv)+(Lπv−Lπv∗)+(Lπv∗−Lπvπ).v^* - v_\pi = (\mathrm{L}_{\pi^*} v^* - \mathrm{L}_{\pi^*} v) + (\mathrm{L}_{\pi^*} v - \BellmanPi v) + (\BellmanPi v - \BellmanPi v^*) + (\BellmanPi v^* - \BellmanPi v_\pi).v∗−vπ​=(Lπ∗​v∗−Lπ∗​v)+(Lπ∗​v−Lπ​v)+(Lπ​v−Lπ​v∗)+(Lπ​v∗−Lπ​vπ​).
(9)

The second term is nonpositive because π\piπ is greedy for vvv. The others are γPπ∗(v∗−v)\gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi^*}(v^* - v)γPπ∗​(v∗−v), γPπ(v−v∗)\gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi(v - v^*)γPπ​(v−v∗) and γPπ(v∗−vπ)\gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi(v^* - v_\pi)γPπ​(v∗−vπ​), and stochastic matrices do not increase the sup norm. Since v∗−vπ≥0v^* - v_\pi \geq 0v∗−vπ​≥0, taking the maximum over states gives ∥v∗−vπ∥∞≤2γ∥v−v∗∥∞+γ∥v∗−vπ∥∞\|v^* - v_\pi\|_\infty \leq 2\gamma\|v - v^*\|_\infty + \gamma\|v^* - v_\pi\|_\infty∥v∗−vπ​∥∞​≤2γ∥v−v∗∥∞​+γ∥v∗−vπ​∥∞​.

Combining the two, the greedy policies of fitted value iteration are eventually within 2γε/(1−γ)22\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)^22γε/(1−γ)2 of optimal. The bound asks nothing of the fit except accuracy: no linearity, no particular basis, no structure at all. This is what licenses a tree ensemble or a neural network in place of a table. It also says where the difficulty lies, in three places that the rest of this chapter and the next ones take up.

  1. The error is measured in the sup norm, at every state. A regression controls an average error over the states where targets were computed, and nothing at the states it never saw. The analysis of fitted value iteration by Munos (2007) and Munos & Szepesvári (2008) replaces the sup norm by weighted norms. The price is a concentrability coefficient, which measures how far the state distributions that policies reach can be from the distribution of the data. It is the theoretical form of the coverage problem of batch and offline reinforcement learning.

  2. The fit must be achievable. The bound needs some θ\thetaθ with v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\theta)v(⋅;θ) close to Lvk\Bellman v_kLvk​ for every vkv_kvk​ the algorithm produces. The function class must therefore be nearly closed under the Bellman operator, not merely able to represent v∗v^*v∗.

  3. The error must stay bounded. The theorem assumes one ε\varepsilonε for all iterations. If the fit error grows with vkv_kvk​, the bound says nothing, and the next section shows that this happens.

When Fitting Diverges, and Which Fits Cannot¶

Can a fit that represents the solution exactly still make value iteration diverge, and which fitting rules rule this out?

A Two-State Counterexample¶

The following example is due to Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1996). There are two states and one action. State 1 moves to state 2, state 2 stays where it is, and all rewards are zero, so v∗=0v^* = 0v∗=0. The value function is represented with a single feature, v(1;θ)=θv(1;\theta) = \thetav(1;θ)=θ and v(2;θ)=2θv(2;\theta) = 2\thetav(2;θ)=2θ, which contains v∗v^*v∗ at θ=0\theta = 0θ=0. Fitted value iteration computes the targets at both states and fits them by least squares with equal weights. Both targets equal γv(2;θk)=2γθk\gamma v(2;\theta_k) = 2\gamma\theta_kγv(2;θk​)=2γθk​, and the fit minimizes (θ−2γθk)2+(2θ−2γθk)2(\theta - 2\gamma\theta_k)^2 + (2\theta - 2\gamma\theta_k)^2(θ−2γθk​)2+(2θ−2γθk​)2, which gives

θk+1=6γ5θk.\theta_{k+1} = \frac{6\gamma}{5}\theta_k.θk+1​=56γ​θk​.
(10)

For γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6 the iterates diverge from every θ0≠0\theta_0 \neq 0θ0​=0. The Bellman operator shrinks the difference between vkv_kvk​ and v∗v^*v∗ by γ\gammaγ, and the fit then stretches it by 6/56/56/5: the target is the constant 2γθk2\gamma\theta_k2γθk​, and the best line through the origin overshoots it at state 2, where it predicts 125γθk\frac{12}{5}\gamma\theta_k512​γθk​. The fit error grows in proportion to θk\theta_kθk​, which is why Theorem 1 does not apply. Boyan & Moore (1995) observed the same failure with polynomial regression and neural networks on small control problems, at a time when TD-Gammon had made neural value functions look easy.

Averagers: Fits That Cannot Expand¶

The counterexample suggests asking which fitting rules cannot stretch differences between functions. The answer was found independently in computational economics Judd (1992)Judd (1996)McGrattan (1997)Santos & Vigo-Aguiar (1998), economic dynamics Stachurski (2009), and reinforcement learning Gordon (1995)Gordon (1999), and the communities arrived at essentially the same conditions.

Proposition 2 (Monotone operators are nonexpansive (Stachurski))

Let P:V→V\Proj: \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{V}P:V→V be a linear operator on the space V\mathcal{V}V of bounded real-valued functions on S\mathcal{S}S. If P\ProjP satisfies:

  1. Monotonicity: f≤gf \leq gf≤g pointwise implies Pf≤Pg\Proj f \leq \Proj gPf≤Pg

  2. Constant preservation: P1=1\Proj\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}P1=1 where 1\mathbf{1}1 is the constant function equal to 1

Then P\ProjP is nonexpansive in the sup norm: ∥Pf−Pg∥∞≤∥f−g∥∞\|\Proj f - \Proj g\|_\infty \leq \|f - g\|_\infty∥Pf−Pg∥∞​≤∥f−g∥∞​ for all f,g∈Vf, g \in \mathcal{V}f,g∈V.

Proof 3

Let M=∥f−g∥∞M = \|f - g\|_\inftyM=∥f−g∥∞​. Then −M≤f(s)−g(s)≤M-M \leq f(s) - g(s) \leq M−M≤f(s)−g(s)≤M for all sss, which can be written as g−M1≤f≤g+M1g - M\mathbf{1} \leq f \leq g + M\mathbf{1}g−M1≤f≤g+M1. By monotonicity, P(g−M1)≤Pf≤P(g+M1)\Proj(g - M\mathbf{1}) \leq \Proj f \leq \Proj(g + M\mathbf{1})P(g−M1)≤Pf≤P(g+M1). By linearity and constant preservation, Pg−M1≤Pf≤Pg+M1\Proj g - M\mathbf{1} \leq \Proj f \leq \Proj g + M\mathbf{1}Pg−M1≤Pf≤Pg+M1, which means ∣Pf(s)−Pg(s)∣≤M|\Proj f(s) - \Proj g(s)| \leq M∣Pf(s)−Pg(s)∣≤M for all sss. Therefore ∥Pf−Pg∥∞≤∥f−g∥∞\|\Proj f - \Proj g\|_\infty \leq \|f - g\|_\infty∥Pf−Pg∥∞​≤∥f−g∥∞​.

A monotone, constant-preserving operator acts like a weighted average: it respects order and cannot amplify differences. For an interpolation operator (Pf)(s)=∑jℓj(s)f(sj)(\Proj f)(s) = \sum_j \ell_j(s) f(s_j)(Pf)(s)=∑j​ℓj​(s)f(sj​) with cardinal functions ℓj\ell_jℓj​, the two conditions say that the weights are nonnegative and sum to one, which is the condition Λ=1\Lambda = 1Λ=1 of the finite-horizon chapter. The least-squares fit of the counterexample violates them: it maps the constant function (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1) to (3/5,6/5)(3/5, 6/5)(3/5,6/5).

Theorem 2 (Stability of projected value iteration (Santos-Vigo-Aguiar))

Let L:V→V\Bellman: \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{V}L:V→V be a γ\gammaγ-contraction on the space V\mathcal{V}V of bounded functions with respect to the sup norm. Let P:V→V\Proj: \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{V}P:V→V be a linear approximation operator satisfying monotonicity and constant preservation.

Then the composed operator PL\Proj \BellmanPL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction, and projected value iteration vk+1=PLvkv_{k+1} = \Proj \Bellman v_kvk+1​=PLvk​ converges globally to a unique fixed point vP∈Range(P)v_\Proj \in \text{Range}(\Proj)vP​∈Range(P) with approximation error:

∥vP−v∗∥∞≤11−γ∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞,\|v_\Proj - v^*\|_\infty \leq \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \|\Proj v^* - v^*\|_\infty,∥vP​−v∗∥∞​≤1−γ1​∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞​,
(11)

where v∗v^*v∗ is the true value function.

Proof 4

By Proposition 2, P\ProjP is nonexpansive. Since L\BellmanL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction,

∥PLf−PLg∥∞≤∥Lf−Lg∥∞≤γ∥f−g∥∞,\|\Proj \Bellman f - \Proj \Bellman g\|_\infty \leq \|\Bellman f - \Bellman g\|_\infty \leq \gamma\|f-g\|_\infty,∥PLf−PLg∥∞​≤∥Lf−Lg∥∞​≤γ∥f−g∥∞​,
(12)

so PL\Proj \BellmanPL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction and Theorem 3 gives the unique fixed point and global convergence. For the error bound, use vP=PLvPv_\Proj = \Proj\Bellman v_\ProjvP​=PLvP​ and v∗=Lv∗v^* = \Bellman v^*v∗=Lv∗:

∥vP−v∗∥∞≤∥PLvP−PLv∗∥∞+∥PLv∗−v∗∥∞≤γ∥vP−v∗∥∞+∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞,\|v_\Proj - v^*\|_\infty \leq \|\Proj\Bellman v_\Proj - \Proj\Bellman v^*\|_\infty + \|\Proj \Bellman v^* - v^*\|_\infty \leq \gamma \|v_\Proj - v^*\|_\infty + \|\Proj v^* - v^*\|_\infty,∥vP​−v∗∥∞​≤∥PLvP​−PLv∗∥∞​+∥PLv∗−v∗∥∞​≤γ∥vP​−v∗∥∞​+∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞​,
(13)

and rearranging gives the claim.

The fixed-point error is the best-approximation error ∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞\|\Proj v^* - v^*\|_\infty∥Pv∗−v∗∥∞​ amplified by (1−γ)−1(1-\gamma)^{-1}(1−γ)−1. For a monotone fit the per-iteration error stays bounded, and the result is the special case of Theorem 1 in which the third difficulty above cannot arise. For a finite state space, the monotonicity conditions describe averaging with nonnegative weights, a characterization due to Gordon.

Definition 1 (Averager (Gordon))

An operator P:R∣S∣→R∣S∣\Proj: \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|} \to \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}|}P:R∣S∣→R∣S∣ is an averager if Pv=Wv\Proj v = WvPv=Wv where WWW is a ∣S∣×∣S∣|\mathcal{S}| \times |\mathcal{S}|∣S∣×∣S∣ stochastic matrix: wij≥0w_{ij} \geq 0wij​≥0 and ∑jwij=1\sum_j w_{ij} = 1∑j​wij​=1 for all iii.

Averagers satisfy the monotonicity conditions: linearity follows from matrix multiplication, monotonicity from nonnegativity of the entries, and constant preservation from the row sums.

Theorem 3 (Stability with averagers (Gordon))

If P\ProjP is an averager and L\BellmanL is the Bellman operator (a γ\gammaγ-contraction), then PL\Proj \BellmanPL is a γ\gammaγ-contraction, and value iteration vk+1=PLvkv_{k+1} = \Proj \Bellman v_kvk+1​=PLvk​ converges to a unique fixed point.

The stochastic matrix gives the averaging a Markov-chain reading: Pv\Proj vPv is an expected value after one random transition, and expectations preserve order. The finite-horizon chapter made the same observation about linear interpolation, which replaces a deterministic successor by a random grid node with the interpolation weights as probabilities. Composing that chain with the model’s own transitions makes PL\Proj\BellmanPL the Bellman operator of a finite-state MDP, which is why it contracts.

Which regressors are averagers? State aggregation, kkk-nearest neighbors, kernel smoothing with nonnegative kernels normalized to sum to one, and multilinear interpolation on a grid all predict a convex combination of training targets whose weights depend only on the states. So does a regression tree, which predicts the average of the targets in a leaf, as long as its partition of the state space does not depend on the targets. Ernst et al. (2005) used this to give tree-based fitted Q-iteration a convergence guarantee. Their extremely randomized trees choose splits with the help of the targets, and freezing the tree structure after some iterations restores the guarantee. Linear least squares, high-order polynomial interpolation, and neural networks are not averagers.

MethodAverager?Notes
Piecewise linear interpolationYesBarycentric weights are nonnegative and sum to one
Multilinear interpolation (grid)YesWeights are products of one-dimensional hat functions
Shape-preserving splines (Schumaker)YesDesigned to maintain monotonicity
State aggregation, kkk-nearest neighborsYesEqual weights within a group or neighborhood
Kernel smoothing (nonnegative kernels)YesIf the weights are normalized to sum to one
Regression trees and forests, fixed partitionYesLeaf averages; guarantee lost if splits depend on the targets
High-order polynomial interpolationNoNegative weights (Runge phenomenon)
Least squares on an arbitrary basisNoThe counterexample above
Neural networksNoNo sign or normalization constraint on the fit

The table puts the methods of this chapter in their place. Collocation with piecewise-linear interpolation is an averager, and the folk wisdom that linear interpolation is safe for value iteration is a theorem. Collocation with the cubic through four Chebyshev nodes is not, and its convergence in the worked example was not guaranteed. Galerkin projection and least squares are not averagers. The tree ensemble in the eight-dimensional example sits on the boundary, and the network is outside.

The solver matters too. Fitted value iteration needs PL\Proj\BellmanPL to contract. Newton’s method does not; its convergence depends on the conditioning of the Jacobian and on the starting point. This is the reason for the hybrid strategy of Step 4: Solve the Finite-Dimensional Problem: a few iterations with a monotone, low-order approximation to get a starting guess, then Newton’s method with a smooth, high-order one.

Exercises: Divergence and Averagers

  1. The counterexample with an averager. Replace the least-squares fit in the two-state example by state aggregation into a single group. Write P\ProjP as a matrix, check that it is an averager, and show that fitted value iteration converges for every γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1. What is its fixed point?

  2. A non-monotone example. Using Lagrange interpolation with 4 equally spaced nodes on [0,1][0, 1][0,1], compute the interpolation weights for the point x=0.1x = 0.1x=0.1. Show that some weights are negative.

  3. Verifying monotonicity. Consider piecewise linear interpolation on a 5-point grid. Write out the interpolation weights for a point between grid points 2 and 3. Verify that all weights are nonnegative and sum to one.

  4. Trees. Show that a regression tree with a fixed partition is an averager. Explain why a tree that chooses its splits by the targets can change its partition from one iteration to the next, and which step of the proof of Theorem 2 this breaks.

On-Policy Weighting Rescues Policy Evaluation¶

The counterexample has a second reading. The chain moves from state 1 to state 2 and stays there, so its stationary distribution puts all its mass on state 2. If the fit weights each state by that distribution, it minimizes (2θ−2γθk)2(2\theta - 2\gamma\theta_k)^2(2θ−2γθk​)2 alone, and θk+1=γθk\theta_{k+1} = \gamma\theta_kθk+1​=γθk​ converges. The equal weighting was the problem: it fits the value at a state the process does not occupy as much as the value at the state it does.

This observation is a theorem for policy evaluation Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1997), proved to explain the convergence of TD(0) with linear features. Take a finite state space S={s1,…,sm}\mathcal{S} = \{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}S={s1​,…,sm​}, a feature matrix Φ∈Rm×n\boldsymbol{\Phi} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}Φ∈Rm×n with rows φ(s)⊤\boldsymbol\varphi(s)^\topφ(s)⊤, and a distribution ξ\xiξ over states with Ξ=diag(ξ)\boldsymbol{\Xi} = \text{diag}(\xi)Ξ=diag(ξ). The ξ\xiξ-weighted inner product, norm, and least-squares projection onto the span of the features are

⟨u,v⟩ξ=u⊤Ξv,∥v∥ξ=v⊤Ξv,P=Φ(Φ⊤ΞΦ)−1Φ⊤Ξ.\langle u, v \rangle_\xi = u^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} v, \qquad \|v\|_\xi = \sqrt{v^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} v}, \qquad \Proj = \boldsymbol{\Phi}(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} \boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi}.⟨u,v⟩ξ​=u⊤Ξv,∥v∥ξ​=v⊤Ξv​,P=Φ(Φ⊤ΞΦ)−1Φ⊤Ξ.
(14)

Fitted policy evaluation is vk+1=PLπvkv_{k+1} = \Proj\BellmanPi v_kvk+1​=PLπ​vk​ with Lπv=rπ+γPπv\BellmanPi v = \mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi vLπ​v=rπ​+γPπ​v. In reinforcement learning the weighting is not a free choice: the states in the data are those the process visits, and if the chain under π\piπ is ergodic their distribution approaches the stationary distribution ξ\xiξ with ξ⊤Pπ=ξ⊤\xi^\top\mathbf{P}_\pi = \xi^\topξ⊤Pπ​=ξ⊤. Suppose that is the weighting. We show that P\ProjP is nonexpansive and Lπ\BellmanPiLπ​ is a γ\gammaγ-contraction, both in ∥⋅∥ξ\|\cdot\|_\xi∥⋅∥ξ​, so that

∥PLπv−PLπw∥ξ≤∥Lπv−Lπw∥ξ≤γ∥v−w∥ξ.\|\Proj \BellmanPi v - \Proj \BellmanPi w\|_\xi \leq \|\BellmanPi v - \BellmanPi w\|_\xi \leq \gamma \|v - w\|_\xi.∥PLπ​v−PLπ​w∥ξ​≤∥Lπ​v−Lπ​w∥ξ​≤γ∥v−w∥ξ​.

The argument of Theorem 2 bounds its distance to vπv_\pivπ​ by (1−γ)−1∥Pvπ−vπ∥ξ(1-\gamma)^{-1}\|\Proj v_\pi - v_\pi\|_\xi(1−γ)−1∥Pvπ​−vπ​∥ξ​, and the inner-product structure improves the constant to (1−γ2)−1/2(1-\gamma^2)^{-1/2}(1−γ2)−1/2 Tsitsiklis & Van Roy (1997).

The on-policy condition. Convergence came from matching the weighting to the operator, not from any property of the fit beyond orthogonality: ξ\xiξ must be the stationary distribution of the very Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ that appears in Lπ\BellmanPiLπ​. When the data are collected by following π\piπ, this holds automatically, which is on-policy learning. When they come from another behavior policy, as in the counterexample’s equal weighting or in learning from a replay buffer filled by older policies, the Jensen step fails, Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ need not be nonexpansive in ∥⋅∥ξ\|\cdot\|_\xi∥⋅∥ξ​, and PLπ\Proj\BellmanPiPLπ​ may not contract. Baird’s counterexample Baird (1995) is the classical demonstration.

The Optimality Operator and the Deadly Triad¶

Can the weighted argument be extended to the optimality operator Lv=max⁡a[ra+γPav]\Bellman v = \max_a [\mathbf{r}_a + \gamma \mathbf{P}_a v]Lv=maxa​[ra​+γPa​v]? Not this way. The obstacle is the Jensen step. For the optimality operator we would need to bound [max⁡a∑s′p(s′∣s,a)z(s′)]2\big[\max_{a} \sum_{s'} p(s'|s,a) z(s')\big]^2[maxa​∑s′​p(s′∣s,a)z(s′)]2, and a maximum of averages is not an average. Nor is there a single stationary distribution to match, since the greedy policy, and with it the state distribution, changes from iteration to iteration.

Sutton & Barto (2018) call the combination of function approximation, bootstrapping (targets built from the current estimate), and off-policy data the deadly triad: any two are manageable, all three can diverge. Fitted Q-iteration with a neural network has all three. There is no general convergence theorem for it, and divergence can be observed on small examples. Yet NFQ and DQN solve many problems, because of design choices that limit the damage: each fit is run against targets held fixed, the fit is warm-started from the previous parameters, a separate target network changes slowly, and a large replay buffer keeps the data distribution from tracking every change of policy. The fitted Q-iteration chapter examines these choices one by one.

Approximate Policy Iteration¶

What does Newton’s method, the other solver of the previous chapter, become when the value function is parametric, and what does the linear case add?

In the exact setting, Newton’s method on the Bellman equation is policy iteration (Newton-Kantorovich and Policy Iteration): by the envelope theorem the Jacobian at vkv_kvk​ involves the transition matrix of the greedy policy πk\pi_kπk​, and the Newton step solves the evaluation equation of πk\pi_kπk​. With a parametric value function the same holds, except that the evaluation is done within the function class. The algorithm alternates approximate evaluation, finding θ\thetaθ with v(⋅;θ)≈vπkv(\cdot;\theta) \approx v_{\pi_k}v(⋅;θ)≈vπk​​, and greedy improvement. This is approximate policy iteration. Its guarantee has the same form as for fitted value iteration: if every evaluation is accurate to ε\varepsilonε in the sup norm, the policies are eventually within 2γε/(1−γ)22\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)^22γε/(1−γ)2 of optimal Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis (1996). Unlike exact policy iteration, the sequence of policies need not improve monotonically, and it can cycle among a few policies.

Two remarks carry over from the exact case. With the smooth Bellman operator, the Jacobian is γPπk\gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_k}γPπk​​ for the softmax policy, with no ties to resolve (Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method). And the recommendation at the end of Step 4: Solve the Finite-Dimensional Problem, a few sweeps of function iteration before switching to Newton, is how Rust solved his bus-engine model (Rust’s Bus Engines and Inverse Reinforcement Learning).

For collocation, the Newton step reads as follows. Let ai∗a_i^*ai∗​ be the greedy action at collocation point sis_isi​ for the current coefficients. The envelope theorem gives the Jacobian of the targets, [J]ij=γ∑s′p(s′∣si,ai∗)φj(s′)[J]_{ij} = \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s'|s_i, a_i^*) \varphi_j(s')[J]ij​=γ∑s′​p(s′∣si​,ai∗​)φj​(s′), and the Newton step solves (Φ−J)θ(k+1)=rπk(\boldsymbol\Phi - J)\theta^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{r}_{\pi_k}(Φ−J)θ(k+1)=rπk​​, the evaluation equation of the greedy policy restricted to the collocation points and solved within the span of the basis.

The Linear Case: LSTD and LSPI¶

When the features enter linearly and the state space is finite, the approximate evaluation step has a closed form. The fixed point of fitted policy evaluation solves the projected Bellman equation (18). Its residual Lπv−v\BellmanPi v - vLπ​v−v is ξ\xiξ-orthogonal to every feature, which in matrix form reads

Φ⊤Ξ(rπ+γPπΦθ−Φθ)=0,that isΦ⊤Ξ(Φ−γPπΦ)θ=Φ⊤Ξrπ.\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi \boldsymbol{\Phi} \theta - \boldsymbol{\Phi} \theta) = \mathbf{0}, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\boldsymbol{\Phi} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi \boldsymbol{\Phi}) \theta = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} \mathbf{r}_\pi.Φ⊤Ξ(rπ​+γPπ​Φθ−Φθ)=0,that isΦ⊤Ξ(Φ−γPπ​Φ)θ=Φ⊤Ξrπ​.
(19)

This is the LSTD (least-squares temporal difference) solution of Bradtke & Barto (1996), an n×nn\times nn×n linear system Aθ=b\mathbf{A}\theta = \mathbf{b}Aθ=b. The practical algorithm never forms Φ\boldsymbol\PhiΦ over all states or Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ explicitly. It accumulates A=Es∼ξ[φ(s)(φ(s)−γφ(s′))⊤]\mathbf{A} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \xi}[\boldsymbol{\varphi}(s)(\boldsymbol{\varphi}(s) - \gamma \boldsymbol{\varphi}(s'))^\top]A=Es∼ξ​[φ(s)(φ(s)−γφ(s′))⊤] and b=Es∼ξ[φ(s)r]\mathbf{b} = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \xi}[\boldsymbol{\varphi}(s) r]b=Es∼ξ​[φ(s)r] from sampled transitions (s,r,s′)(s, r, s')(s,r,s′), which is possible because the system is linear in the unknown.

Check that the dimensions work out: with mmm states and nnn features, what are the dimensions of Φ\boldsymbol{\Phi}Φ, Ξ\boldsymbol{\Xi}Ξ, Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​, and A\mathbf{A}A?

On a 3-state chain under a fixed policy, with Pπ=(0.70.20.10.30.40.30.10.30.6)\mathbf{P}_\pi = \begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}Pπ​=⎝⎛​0.70.30.1​0.20.40.3​0.10.30.6​⎠⎞​, rπ=(1,2,0)\mathbf{r}_\pi = (1, 2, 0)rπ​=(1,2,0), features φ(s)=(1,s)\varphi(s) = (1, s)φ(s)=(1,s) and uniform weights:

P_pi = np.array([[0.7, 0.2, 0.1], [0.3, 0.4, 0.3], [0.1, 0.3, 0.6]])

# Uniform weighting
xi = np.ones(3) / 3
Xi = np.diag(xi)

# LSTD matrices
A = Phi.T @ Xi @ (Phi - gamma * P_pi @ Phi)
b = Phi.T @ Xi @ r_pi

theta_lstd = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
v_lstd = Phi @ theta_lstd
v_exact = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(3) - gamma * P_pi, r_pi)

print(f"LSTD solution: theta = ({theta_lstd[0]:.4f}, {theta_lstd[1]:.4f})")
print(f"\n{'State':<8} {'Exact':<12} {'LSTD':<12} {'Error':<12}")
print("-" * 44)
for s in range(3):
    print(f"{s+1:<8} {v_exact[s]:<12.4f} {v_lstd[s]:<12.4f} {v_lstd[s] - v_exact[s]:<12.4f}")

# Verify orthogonality
residual = r_pi + gamma * P_pi @ v_lstd - v_lstd
print(f"\nGalerkin orthogonality: <residual, phi_1> = {np.sum(xi * residual * Phi[:,0]):.6f}")
LSTD solution: theta = (12.2772, -0.9901)

With the max back in, Newton’s method on the projected optimality equation Φ⊤Ξ(L(Φθ)−Φθ)=0\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi}\big(\Bellman(\boldsymbol\Phi\theta) - \boldsymbol{\Phi} \theta\big) = \mathbf{0}Φ⊤Ξ(L(Φθ)−Φθ)=0 uses the envelope-theorem Jacobian Φ⊤Ξ(γPπkΦ−Φ)\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_k} \boldsymbol{\Phi} - \boldsymbol{\Phi})Φ⊤Ξ(γPπk​​Φ−Φ) at the greedy policy πk\pi_kπk​. After the terms in θ(k)\theta^{(k)}θ(k) cancel, the Newton step is

Φ⊤Ξ(Φ−γPπkΦ) θ(k+1)=Φ⊤Ξrπk,\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\boldsymbol{\Phi} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_k} \boldsymbol{\Phi})\, \theta^{(k+1)} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} \mathbf{r}_{\pi_k},Φ⊤Ξ(Φ−γPπk​​Φ)θ(k+1)=Φ⊤Ξrπk​​,
(20)

the LSTD system for πk\pi_kπk​. Alternating greedy improvement with LSTD evaluation is LSPI (least-squares policy iteration) Lagoudakis & Parr (2003). Compare it with fitted value iteration in the same coordinates, Φ⊤ΞΦ θ(k+1)=Φ⊤Ξ(rπk+γPπkΦθ(k))\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} \boldsymbol{\Phi}\, \theta^{(k+1)} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top \boldsymbol{\Xi} (\mathbf{r}_{\pi_k} + \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_k} \boldsymbol{\Phi} \theta^{(k)})Φ⊤ΞΦθ(k+1)=Φ⊤Ξ(rπk​​+γPπk​​Φθ(k)): both use the greedy policy, but fitted value iteration applies its Bellman operator once and regresses, while LSPI solves for its value.

The closed forms need the features to enter linearly. With a neural network, the evaluation step has no closed form, and the natural replacement is a few sweeps of fitted policy evaluation, q←PLπqq \leftarrow \Proj\BellmanPi qq←PLπ​q, which is what the critic of NFQCA does.

Exercises: LSTD and LSPI

  1. Computing the stationary distribution. For the 3-state chain above, compute the stationary distribution ξ\xiξ satisfying ξ⊤Pπ=ξ⊤\xi^\top \mathbf{P}_\pi = \xi^\topξ⊤Pπ​=ξ⊤.

  2. LSTD with stationary weighting. Recompute the LSTD solution using the stationary distribution instead of uniform weighting. Compare the approximation error.

  3. Two updates. On a small MDP with two actions and linear features, implement fitted value iteration and LSPI (20). Compare the number of iterations, and find features under which LSPI cycles between two policies.

From Fitted Value Iteration to FQI and NFQCA¶

Which steps separate the algorithm of this chapter from the fitted Q-iteration methods used in practice, and where is each taken?

Fitted value iteration, as stated here, assumes four things that NFQCA does not.

It learns values of states, not of actions. To act greedily with respect to v(⋅;θ)v(\cdot;\theta)v(⋅;θ) requires, at every decision, the expectation r(s,a)+γ E[v(s′;θ)∣s,a]r(s,a) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[v(s';\theta) \mid s,a]r(s,a)+γE[v(s′;θ)∣s,a] for every action: the model and an integral at decision time. Storing an action-value function q(s,a;θ)q(s,a;\theta)q(s,a;θ) instead moves that work into training, so that acting is a maximization over q(s,⋅;θ)q(s,\cdot;\theta)q(s,⋅;θ). The Bellman operator on qqq-functions, (Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ E[max⁡a′q(s′,a′)∣s,a](\Bellman q)(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[\max_{a'} q(s',a') \mid s,a](Lq)(s,a)=r(s,a)+γE[maxa′​q(s′,a′)∣s,a], is again a γ\gammaγ-contraction, and everything in this chapter applies to it unchanged. Fitted value iteration on qqq is fitted Q-iteration.

It computes expectations exactly. The targets contain E[ ⋅∣s,a]\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot \mid s,a]E[⋅∣s,a], which the eight-dimensional example already replaced by an average over draws. With a simulator, or with logged data, a target typically uses a single sampled successor. The Monte Carlo chapter studies what this costs: variance, and a bias that comes from maximizing over noisy estimates.

It chooses the states at which targets are computed. Batch reinforcement learning receives a fixed set of transitions instead, and online reinforcement learning a buffer that changes as the agent acts. The error analysis of this chapter said that a fit is controlled only where there are data. The fitted Q-iteration chapter builds the batch algorithms on this template, the tree-based FQI of Ernst et al. (2005) (an averager) and NFQ Riedmiller (2005) (a neural network), and then DQN, whose design choices respond to the deadly triad.

It maximizes over a finite set of actions. Every target contains max⁡a′q(s′,a′;θ)\max_{a'} q(s',a';\theta)maxa′​q(s′,a′;θ). When the action is continuous, a torque or a dose, that maximum is a nonlinear program, to be solved once for every target at every iteration. NFQCA Hafner & Riedmiller (2011) trains a second network, an actor πw(s)≈arg⁡max⁡aq(s,a;θ)\pi_{\boldsymbol w}(s) \approx \arg\max_a q(s,a;\theta)πw​(s)≈argmaxa​q(s,a;θ), and uses it in the target in place of the maximum. The critic qqq is fitted by regression against fixed targets, exactly as in this chapter, and the actor by gradient ascent on the critic. In the terms of Approximate Policy Iteration, NFQCA is approximate policy iteration with one fitted evaluation sweep per improvement, that is, a fitted version of modified policy iteration (Algorithm 4) in which the improvement step is learned as well. The amortized action optimization chapter develops it, together with its online descendants DDPG and TD3. The smooth Bellman operator meets the same obstacle in the partition function over a continuous action set (Continuous Action and State Spaces), and soft actor-critic resolves it in the same way.

Summary and Outlook¶

Replacing the table by a parametric function turns value iteration into fitted value iteration: compute Bellman targets at chosen states, fit the function to them, repeat. Collocation and Galerkin projection are two fitting rules, and regression with trees or neural networks is the one that scales, as the eight-dimensional stopping problem showed. If each fit is accurate to ε\varepsilonε in the sup norm, the value error stays below ε/(1−γ)\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)ε/(1−γ) and the greedy policy loses at most 2γε/(1−γ)22\gamma\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)^22γε/(1−γ)2. The fit can, however, stretch differences and make the iteration diverge, even when it represents the solution exactly. Averagers cannot, and for policy evaluation, least squares weighted by the stationary distribution of the policy cannot either. Neither argument covers the optimality operator with a neural network, which is the setting of practical fitted Q-iteration. Newton’s method becomes approximate policy iteration, with LSTD and LSPI as its linear case.

Exact target evaluation still assumes access to the transition probabilities or an exact expectation. How can the same Bellman update be estimated when the model supplies only samples? Monte Carlo Bellman estimation replaces the exact integral by sampled averages and makes their variance and maximization bias explicit.

Self-checks¶

Exercise 1 (Weighting shift)

If the fitting distribution puts almost no mass on an important region of the state space, what failure should you expect?

Solution to Exercise 1

The fit may be accurate under the weighted norm yet poor in that neglected region, leading to bad values or decisions there. In the error bound of fitted value iteration, this shows up as a large sup-norm error, or, in the weighted analysis, as a large concentrability coefficient.

Exercise 2 (Accurate fits, bad iteration)

In the two-state counterexample, the function class contains v∗v^*v∗ exactly. Why does fitted value iteration still diverge, and why does Theorem 1 not prevent it?

Solution to Exercise 2

The least-squares fit is not an averager: it stretches the constant target into a line that overshoots at state 2, by a factor 6/56/56/5, which beats the contraction γ\gammaγ when γ>5/6\gamma > 5/6γ>5/6. The fit error at iteration kkk is proportional to θk\theta_kθk​, so there is no single ε\varepsilonε that bounds it for all kkk, and the theorem’s assumption fails.

Exercise 3 (Where the actor enters)

Which part of fitted Q-iteration does the actor of NFQCA replace, and why is it needed only for continuous actions?

Solution to Exercise 3

It replaces the maximization over next actions inside each Bellman target. With a finite action set the maximum is computed by enumeration; with a continuous action set it is a nonlinear program for every target, and the actor amortizes those programs into one trained network.
